learn: Some information in a text is explicit: the author states it directly.
An inference is a conclusion you reach by combining clues in the text with what you already know. If a character's umbrella drips as she walks in, you can infer it's raining.
Good readers make inferences and support them with evidence from the text.
check: A conclusion from clues plus what you know
A sentence copied word for word
A dripping umbrella lets you infer that...
lessons.try: Read a page of a story and write one inference with the clue that supports it.

learn: When you use evidence, you can quote the author's exact words inside quotation marks.
Introduce quotes with phrases like "The text states..." or "According to the author...".
Then explain how the quote supports your idea.
check: Explain how it supports your idea
lessons.try: Choose a quote from your book that shows a character's feelings and explain it.

learn: Annotating means marking a text as you read: underlining key ideas, circling new words and writing notes in the margins.
Symbols can help: ? for confusing parts, ! for surprises, * for important ideas.
Annotations make it easier to find evidence later.
check: Marking a text as you read
lessons.try: Annotate a short article using at least three different symbols.

learn: Close reading means reading a short text several times with a purpose.
First read for the gist, second for details, third for the author's craft.
Each read shows you something new.
check: Close reading means reading a text...
The first read is for the...
The third read looks at the author's...
lessons.try: Read a short passage three times, noting something new each time.

learn: Explicit information is stated directly.
Implicit information must be inferred from clues.
Good readers notice both.
lessons.try: Mark explicit facts in blue and inferences in green.

learn: Inference = text clues + what you know.
Use at least two clues for a strong inference.
Say "I can infer... because the text says..."
check: An inference uses text clues plus...
Strong inferences use at least ___ clues.
Start with "I can infer... because the ___ says."
lessons.try: Write three inferences with two clues each.

learn: A quotation copies the author's exact words.
Use quotation marks and the page number.
Quotes prove your ideas.
check: A quote uses the author's ___ words.
lessons.try: Find two quotes that support an idea.

learn: Paraphrasing puts the author's idea in your own words.
Keep the meaning but change the wording.
Still give credit.
lessons.try: Paraphrase three quotes.

learn: Lead into evidence: "According to the text..." "The author states..."
Then explain what it shows.
Evidence + explanation = strong answer.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph using evidence starters.

learn: Annotating means marking the text as you read.
Use symbols: ? for questions, ! for surprises, * for important.
Notes in the margin capture thinking.
lessons.try: Annotate a page with five symbols.

learn: Text-dependent questions need the text to answer.
Go back and find the part that answers.
Restate the question, answer, cite, explain (RACE).
check: RACE stands for Restate, Answer, Cite and...
lessons.try: Answer three questions using RACE.

learn: Authors don't say everything.
Silences, actions and details hint at more.
"She looked away and didn't answer" says a lot.
check: "She looked away and didn't answer" suggests she...
lessons.try: Explain what a character's silence suggests.

learn: Poems pack meaning into few words.
Read aloud, notice repeated words and images.
Ask what feeling the poem creates.
lessons.try: Close-read a short poem and share one discovery.

learn: In discussions, back up ideas with the text.
Build on others: "I agree because..." "I see it differently because..."
Point to the page.
lessons.try: Hold a text-based discussion.

learn: Read closely, infer, quote and paraphrase.
Annotate and use RACE.
Evidence makes your thinking strong.
lessons.try: Complete a close-reading task on a new passage.

learn: The theme is the message or life lesson of a story. It is usually not stated directly.
Themes are big ideas like "friendship takes effort" or "honesty is important".
To find a theme, ask: What did the main character learn? What does the author want readers to understand?
check: The message or life lesson of a story
Which question helps find a theme?
What did the main character learn?
lessons.try: Name the theme of a story you've read recently and explain how you know.

learn: A topic is a word or phrase, like "courage". A theme is a full sentence about the topic, like "Courage means acting even when you're afraid".
Different stories can share a topic but have different themes.
State themes as complete sentences.
check: Courage means acting even when afraid
Can stories share a topic but have different themes?
lessons.try: Turn the topic "kindness" into a theme statement.

learn: A fiction summary tells who, wants, but, so, then: Somebody wanted something, but there was a problem, so they did something, then it ended a certain way.
Keep it short and in your own words.
Leave out minor details and your opinions.
check: In "Somebody Wanted But So Then", "But" is the...
A summary should include your opinion.
Short and in your own words
lessons.try: Use "Somebody, Wanted, But, So, Then" to summarise a fairy tale.

learn: Theme is the big message or lesson of a story.
It's usually not stated; you infer it.
Themes apply to life: "Honesty builds trust."
lessons.try: Name the theme of a fable.

learn: A topic is one or two words: friendship.
A theme is a full statement: True friends stand by you in hard times.
Turn topics into themes.
check: "True friends stand by you" is a...
lessons.try: Turn five topics into theme statements.

learn: Look at how the main character changes.
What lesson did they learn?
That lesson often points to the theme.
check: Theme often comes from what the character...
Look at how the main character...
A greedy character who learns to share suggests the theme...
lessons.try: Track a character's change and infer the theme.

learn: How a conflict is solved reveals theme.
If teamwork solves it, the theme might be about cooperation.
Ask: What helped the character succeed?
check: How a conflict is solved reveals...
If teamwork solves it, the theme is about...
lessons.try: Analyse a conflict's solution for theme.

learn: Titles and repeated objects can hint at theme.
A recurring broken clock might suggest time running out.
Ask why the author chose them.
lessons.try: Explain a symbol in a story.

learn: Stories can have more than one theme.
Charlotte's Web: friendship and the cycle of life.
Support each with evidence.
lessons.try: Find two themes in one story.

learn: Some themes appear in stories everywhere: good vs evil, courage, belonging.
They're called universal.
Compare how cultures show them.
lessons.try: Compare a universal theme in two cultures' tales.

learn: A summary is short, objective and in order.
Include main events and characters.
Leave out opinions and small details.
lessons.try: Rate three summaries and pick the best.

learn: Include characters, setting, problem, key events and solution.
Use transitions: first, then, eventually, finally.
Aim for five to seven sentences.
lessons.try: Summarise a chapter book.

learn: End your summary with the theme.
"In the end, Maya learns that courage means facing fear."
This shows deep understanding.
check: "Maya learns that courage means facing fear" states the...
lessons.try: Add a theme sentence to a summary.

learn: Two stories can share a theme in different ways.
Compare how characters learn it.
Use a chart.
lessons.try: Compare the theme of two stories.

learn: Theme is the message. Summary is the short retelling.
Both rely on understanding the whole story.
Use evidence for theme and objectivity for summary.
lessons.try: Write a summary with a theme for a new story.

learn: Authors reveal characters through their words, thoughts, actions, appearance and how others react to them.
Characters can be round (complex, with many traits) or flat (simple).
A dynamic character changes during the story; a static character stays the same.
check: A complex character with many traits is...
lessons.try: Describe a main character's thoughts, words and actions in one chart.

learn: Setting includes the place, time and mood.
A setting can create problems: a blizzard might trap characters.
Changing the setting would change the story.
lessons.try: Imagine your favourite story in a different setting. How would it change?

learn: Plot follows a pattern: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.
The exposition introduces characters and setting. Rising action builds tension. The climax is the turning point.
Falling action and resolution show what happens after the climax.
check: The turning point of a story is the...
lessons.try: Draw a plot diagram for a story and label each part.

learn: Characters' thoughts reveal what they really feel.
"I'll never be as good as her, Sam thought."
Thoughts can differ from words.
lessons.try: Find a moment where a character thinks one thing and says another.

learn: How others react tells about a character.
If everyone avoids someone, why?
Reactions are clues.
lessons.try: Analyse how others treat a character.

learn: Characters can have hidden motives.
A character may help for selfish reasons.
Look closely at actions and results.
check: Helping for selfish reasons is a ___ motive.
lessons.try: Find a character with a hidden motive.

learn: Characters affect each other.
A mentor guides a hero. A rival pushes them.
Interactions move the plot.
lessons.try: Map how two characters change each other.

learn: Mood is the feeling a setting creates.
A creaky old house = spooky mood. A sunny beach = cheerful mood.
Authors choose details to set mood.
check: Mood is the ___ a setting creates.
A creaky old house creates a ___ mood.
lessons.try: Rewrite a setting to change its mood.

learn: Settings can be obstacles: storms, deserts, strange cities.
Characters must survive or adapt.
Setting shapes the plot.
lessons.try: Find a story where setting causes the problem.

learn: Stories set in the past show how people lived.
Details like clothes, travel and jobs show the time.
Readers learn history through fiction.
lessons.try: List details that show a story's time period.

learn: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
Exposition introduces characters and setting.
The climax is the turning point.
lessons.try: Map a story on a plot diagram.

learn: Character vs character, vs nature, vs self, vs society.
Inner conflict is a struggle inside the character.
Many stories have more than one.
check: A struggle inside a character is ___ conflict.
A shipwreck survival is character vs...
Two rivals fighting is character vs...
lessons.try: Identify conflicts in three stories.

learn: Events cause other events.
"Because she lost the map, they got lost."
Chains of cause and effect drive the plot.
check: "Because she lost the map, they got lost" shows...
Chains of cause and effect drive the...
lessons.try: Make a cause-effect chain for a story.

learn: A flashback jumps to an earlier time.
Foreshadowing hints at what will happen later.
Both add depth and suspense.
check: A flashback goes to an ___ time.
lessons.try: Find a flashback or foreshadowing in a book.

learn: Characters, setting and events work together.
Characters change; settings set mood; plots follow a structure.
Analyse how each affects the others.
check: Mood is the ___ of a setting.
A struggle inside a character is ___ conflict.
lessons.try: Write an analysis of how setting affects a character.

learn: Poems are written in lines and stanzas (groups of lines).
Many poems use rhythm (a beat) and rhyme (matching end sounds).
Free verse poems don't follow a set rhyme or rhythm.
check: A group of lines in a poem is a...
A poem without set rhyme or rhythm is...
lessons.try: Read Robert Louis Stevenson's "My Shadow" (1885) and count its stanzas.

learn: Plays are written to be performed. They have a cast of characters, dialogue and stage directions.
Stage directions, often in italics or brackets, tell actors how to move and speak.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes.
check: What tells actors how to move?
The list of characters is the...
lessons.try: Write a short scene with two characters and stage directions.

learn: Stories use paragraphs and chapters. Poems use lines and stanzas. Plays use dialogue and scenes.
The same story could be told in any of these forms.
Each form has strengths: poems are compact and musical; plays are meant to be seen.
check: Which is written to be performed?
Can the same story be told in different forms?
lessons.try: Rewrite a short fable as a short poem.

learn: Poems are written in lines and stanzas.
A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph.
Line breaks create rhythm and pause.
check: A group of lines in a poem is a...
lessons.try: Count lines and stanzas in a poem.

learn: Rhythm is the beat of a poem.
Metre is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.
Clap the beat as you read.
check: Rhythm is the ___ of a poem.
Metre is a regular ___ of syllables.
lessons.try: Clap the rhythm of a nursery rhyme.

learn: A rhyme scheme labels rhyming lines with letters: AABB or ABAB.
Lines that rhyme share a letter.
Not all poems rhyme.
lessons.try: Label the rhyme scheme of three poems.

learn: Free verse has no fixed rhyme or metre.
It sounds like natural speech.
Poets still choose words carefully.
lessons.try: Write a free verse poem about rain.

learn: Alliteration repeats starting sounds: "slippery slimy snake."
Onomatopoeia imitates sounds: buzz, crash.
Sound devices make poems fun to read aloud.
check: Sound devices make poems fun to...
lessons.try: Write lines with alliteration and onomatopoeia.

learn: Imagery uses sense words to create pictures.
"Crisp golden leaves crunch underfoot."
Strong images make poems memorable.
check: "Crisp golden leaves crunch" appeals to sight and...
lessons.try: Underline images in a poem and sketch one.

learn: Plays are written to be performed.
They have a cast of characters, dialogue and stage directions.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes.
check: Plays are divided into acts and...
The list of characters is the...
lessons.try: Read a short play aloud in groups.

learn: Stage directions tell actors how to move and speak.
They are often in italics or brackets: (whispering).
They are not spoken aloud.
check: Stage directions tell actors how to...
lessons.try: Add stage directions to a scene.

learn: In plays, the character's name comes before their lines.
No quotation marks are used.
Actors bring the words to life.
check: In plays, the character's ___ comes before lines.
lessons.try: Perform a scene with expression.

learn: Prose is ordinary writing in sentences and paragraphs.
Poetry uses lines and stanzas. Drama uses dialogue and stage directions.
Each form tells stories differently.
lessons.try: Sort text samples into prose, poetry and drama.

learn: A story can be told as prose, a poem or a play.
Compare how each form shows characters and events.
Form changes the reader's experience.
check: A story can be told in ___ forms.
Turning a story into a play needs...
lessons.try: Turn a short story scene into a play.

learn: Poems use lines, rhythm, sound and imagery.
Plays use dialogue, cast, acts, scenes and stage directions.
Prose uses paragraphs.
lessons.try: Perform a poem or play for the class.

learn: In first-person point of view, the narrator is a character in the story and uses "I" and "me".
Readers only know what the narrator thinks and sees.
First person can feel personal and close.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph from a story in first person.

learn: In third person, the narrator is outside the story and uses "he", "she" and "they".
Third-person limited follows one character's thoughts. Third-person omniscient knows all characters' thoughts.
Omniscient means "all-knowing".
lessons.try: Identify the point of view in three books on your shelf.

learn: The same event can look very different from two points of view.
A firsthand account is told by someone who was there. A secondhand account is told by someone who wasn't.
Comparing accounts helps you understand events more fully.
check: A firsthand account is told by...
A news article about something the reporter didn't see is...
lessons.try: Compare a diary entry about an event with a news article about the same event.

learn: The narrator tells the story.
Point of view is the narrator's position.
Ask: Is the narrator in the story or outside it?
check: Point of view is the narrator's...
Ask if the narrator is in the story or...
lessons.try: Identify narrators in three books.

learn: First person uses I, me, we.
The narrator is a character in the story.
We only know what they know.
check: In first person, we know only what the narrator...
lessons.try: Rewrite a third-person paragraph in first person.

learn: First person feels personal and close.
Readers share the narrator's thoughts and feelings.
But the narrator might be wrong or biased.
lessons.try: Discuss if a narrator can be trusted.

learn: Third person uses he, she, they.
Limited means we follow one character's thoughts.
The narrator is outside the story.
check: The third-person narrator is ___ the story.
lessons.try: Find a third-person limited book.

learn: Omniscient means all-knowing.
The narrator knows every character's thoughts.
It gives a wide view of the story.
lessons.try: Find an omniscient passage.

learn: Second person uses "you."
It's rare in stories but common in instructions and choose-your-path books.
It puts the reader in the action.
check: Second person puts the reader in the...
lessons.try: Write a short second-person adventure.

lessons.t: How Point of View Shapes a Story
learn: The same events feel different from different views.
A villain might be a hero from their view.
Point of view controls what readers know.
check: Point of view controls what readers...
A villain might be a ___ from their view.
Same events feel ___ from different views.
lessons.try: Retell a scene from another character's view.

learn: Compare a first-hand account and a second-hand account of an event.
A first-hand account is by someone who was there.
A second-hand account is by someone who learned about it.
check: A first-hand account is by someone who...
A textbook is usually a ___ account.
lessons.try: Compare an eyewitness diary and a textbook about the same event.

learn: Your own views affect how you read.
You might agree or disagree with a narrator.
Explain why with evidence.
lessons.try: Write whether you agree with a narrator's choices.

learn: Poems also have speakers.
The speaker may not be the poet.
Ask: Who is speaking and to whom?
check: The voice in a poem is the...
The speaker may not be the...
Ask who is speaking and to...
lessons.try: Identify the speaker in two poems.

lessons.t: Writing From Different Points of View
learn: Choose a point of view on purpose.
First person for feelings; third for a bigger picture.
Stay consistent.
lessons.try: Write the same scene in first and third person.

learn: First, second and third person.
Limited vs omniscient.
First-hand vs second-hand accounts.
lessons.try: Make a point-of-view chart with examples.

units.t: Main Idea and Text Structure in Nonfiction

learn: Longer texts have a main idea for the whole piece and main ideas for each section.
Headings often hint at section main ideas.
Combine section ideas to find the overall main idea.
check: Do longer texts have more than one main idea?
Yes, one per section plus overall
lessons.try: List the main idea of each section of an article, then the overall main idea.

learn: Chronological structure tells events in time order.
Compare and contrast shows similarities and differences. Cause and effect explains why things happen.
Problem and solution presents a problem and ways to solve it.
check: "Because of the drought, crops failed" shows...
Which structure presents a problem and ways to fix it?
lessons.try: Find an example of each structure in a science or history book.

learn: Charts, graphs, diagrams and timelines give information visually.
Read titles, labels and keys carefully.
Explain how a visual adds to the text.
check: What should you read carefully on a chart?
lessons.try: Find a diagram in a nonfiction book and explain what it adds.

learn: Before reading, preview the title, headings, pictures and captions.
Predict what you'll learn.
Previewing sets a purpose.
lessons.try: Preview an article and write two predictions.

learn: Each section has its own main idea.
The heading often hints at it.
List each section's main idea.
check: Each ___ has its own main idea.
The ___ often hints at a section's main idea.
Section main ideas build the ___ main idea.
lessons.try: Write the main idea of each section of an article.

learn: Some texts have two main ideas.
An article about bees may explain how they make honey and why they're in danger.
Support each with details.
check: An article on bees could cover honey and...
lessons.try: Find two main ideas in one article.

learn: Don't just list details. Explain how they support.
"This detail shows that..."
Connect each detail to the main idea.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph explaining how two details support a main idea.

learn: Chronological texts tell events in time order.
Dates and times are clues.
Biographies and histories often use it.
lessons.try: Make a timeline from a biography.

learn: Comparison texts show likenesses and differences.
Clue words: similarly, both, whereas, on the other hand.
Use a Venn diagram or T-chart.
lessons.try: Compare two animals from an article.

learn: Cause/effect texts explain why things happen.
Clue words: because, therefore, consequently, led to.
Some causes have many effects.
lessons.try: Draw a cause-effect map for an article on erosion.

learn: These texts state a problem and solutions.
Clue words: problem, solution, solved, one answer is.
Evaluate which solution works best.
check: Problem/solution texts give ___ to a problem.
lessons.try: Read about a problem and rank the solutions.

learn: Charts organise information in rows and columns.
Read the title, column headings and row labels.
Charts make comparisons easy.
lessons.try: Answer five questions from a chart.

learn: Diagrams show parts or processes.
Labels name parts. Arrows show steps.
Diagrams explain what words can't.
lessons.try: Explain a diagram of the water cycle.

learn: Combine information from words and visuals.
A graph might add numbers the text didn't give.
Explain how the visual helps.
lessons.try: Write how a graph adds to an article.

learn: Find main ideas and how details support them.
Identify text structures by clue words.
Use charts and diagrams.
lessons.try: Analyse a new article for main idea, structure and visuals.

learn: Many English words come from Greek and Latin roots.
"Tele" means far (telephone, television). "Graph" means write (autograph). "Port" means carry (transport).
"Bio" means life (biology). "Aud" means hear (audience).
lessons.try: List three words with each root: tele, port, bio.

learn: Definition clues give the meaning directly: "A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants, ..."
Synonym and antonym clues give similar or opposite words.
Example clues list examples of the word.
check: "A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants" is a...
An antonym clue gives a word that means...
lessons.try: Find a new word in your reading and name the kind of context clue that helps.

learn: A dictionary gives definitions, pronunciation and parts of speech.
A thesaurus gives synonyms and antonyms.
A glossary defines words used in one book.
check: A glossary defines words used in...
lessons.try: Look up one word in a dictionary and a thesaurus. Compare.

learn: graph means "write" or "draw."
Autograph, paragraph, photograph, biography.
Roots help unlock meanings.
lessons.try: List five graph words and their meanings.

learn: tele means "far." phon means "sound."
Telephone = far sound. Telescope = see far.
Microphone = small sound made bigger.
lessons.try: Build words with tele and phon.

learn: bio means "life." geo means "earth."
Biology = study of life. Geology = study of earth.
-ology means "study of."
lessons.try: Make an -ology list.

learn: port means "carry." rupt means "break."
Transport, portable. Erupt, interrupt.
A volcano erupts: it breaks out.
lessons.try: Sort port and rupt words.

learn: spect means "look." dict means "say."
Inspect, spectator. Predict, dictionary.
Predict = say before.
lessons.try: Use spect and dict words in sentences.

learn: struct means "build." scrib/script means "write."
Construct, structure. Describe, manuscript.
Roots appear in many science and history words.
lessons.try: Find struct and scrib words in a textbook.

learn: uni = one, bi = two, tri = three, quad = four.
Unicycle, bicycle, tricycle, quadrilateral.
Number prefixes appear in maths and science.
lessons.try: Make a chart of number prefix words.

learn: Authors sometimes define a word right in the sentence.
"A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants, ..."
Look for commas, dashes and "or."
check: "A herbivore, an animal that eats only plants" gives a...
lessons.try: Find definition clues in an article.

learn: Examples hint at meaning: "Reptiles, such as snakes and lizards..."
Contrasts show opposites: "Unlike his timid sister, Leo was bold."
Clue words: such as, unlike, but, however.
check: "Unlike his timid sister, Leo was bold." Timid means...
lessons.try: Identify example and contrast clues.

learn: Many words have several meanings: bat, bark, light.
Context tells which meaning fits.
A dictionary lists all meanings.
check: "The dog's bark was loud." Bark means...
lessons.try: Write sentences showing two meanings of five words.

learn: Synonyms mean the same: big, huge.
Antonyms mean the opposite: big, tiny.
A thesaurus lists synonyms and antonyms.
lessons.try: Find three synonyms and an antonym for "happy."

learn: Greek and Latin roots, prefixes and suffixes unlock words.
Context clues help with unknown words.
Use references to check.
lessons.try: Decode ten new science words.

learn: A simile compares two things using "like" or "as": "Her smile was as bright as the sun."
A metaphor compares without those words: "The classroom was a zoo."
Both help readers picture ideas in fresh ways.
check: "As bright as the sun" is a...
"The classroom was a zoo" is a...
lessons.try: Write two similes and two metaphors about the weather.

learn: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: "The wind whispered."
Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration: "I've told you a million times!"
Writers use these for effect and humour.
check: "I've told you a million times" is...
lessons.try: Write a sentence with personification about your house.

learn: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning differs from its words: "It's raining cats and dogs" means it's raining hard.
An adage or proverb is a well-known saying with advice: "Don't count your chickens before they hatch."
Context helps you understand idioms.
check: "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" is a...
lessons.try: Ask family members for their favourite idioms and what they mean.

learn: Literal language means exactly what it says.
Figurative language uses words in creative, non-literal ways.
"It's raining cats and dogs" is figurative.
lessons.try: Sort sentences into literal and figurative.

learn: A simile compares using like or as.
"Her smile was as bright as the sun."
Similes help readers picture things.
check: "As bright as the sun" is a...
lessons.try: Write five similes about your school.

learn: A metaphor compares without like or as.
"The classroom was a zoo."
It says one thing is another.
check: "The classroom was a zoo" is a...
lessons.try: Turn similes into metaphors.

learn: An extended metaphor continues through several lines.
"Life is a journey" with roads, turns and maps.
Poems often use them.
check: An extended metaphor continues through ___ lines.
lessons.try: Write an extended metaphor of school as a ship.

learn: Personification gives human traits to non-human things.
"The wind whispered through the trees."
It makes descriptions lively.
lessons.try: Personify five objects in the room.

learn: Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration.
"I've told you a million times!"
It shows strong feeling or humour.
check: "I've told you a million times" is...
lessons.try: Write three hyperboles about homework.

learn: Idioms are phrases with meanings different from their words.
"Break a leg" means good luck.
Learn idioms through context.
check: Idioms mean something ___ from their words.
lessons.try: Illustrate the literal and real meanings of an idiom.

learn: Adages are short, wise sayings.
"Don't count your chickens before they hatch."
They give advice.
check: "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" means...
Don't plan on something before it happens
lessons.try: Explain five proverbs.

learn: An allusion refers to a famous story, person or event.
"He's a real Scrooge" refers to A Christmas Carol.
Readers need background to get allusions.
check: "He's a real Scrooge" means he is...
An allusion refers to a famous...
lessons.try: Find the source of five allusions.

learn: Poets use figurative language to create images and feelings.
Find similes, metaphors and personification in poems.
Explain what each adds.
check: Poets use figurative language to create...
lessons.try: Analyse figurative language in a poem.

learn: Use figurative language to make writing vivid.
Don't overdo it.
Choose fresh comparisons, not clichés.
lessons.try: Revise a paragraph with two fresh figures of speech.

learn: Similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, idioms, adages and allusions.
They add meaning beyond the literal.
Interpret them from context.
check: "As quiet as a mouse" is a...
lessons.try: Play figurative language bingo.

learn: Relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) connect details: "The girl who won is my friend."
Progressive verbs show ongoing action: I am walking, I was walking, I will be walking.
Use "who" for people and "which" or "that" for things.
lessons.try: Write three sentences using who, which and that.

learn: Modal verbs show possibility or necessity: can, may, must, should, might.
Prepositional phrases begin with a preposition and show relationships: under the bridge, after lunch.
These add precise meaning.
lessons.try: Write a sentence with a modal verb and a prepositional phrase.

learn: Their (belonging), there (place) and they're (they are) are often confused.
To, too and two are also confused: to the store, too hot, two cats.
Use a comma before "and", "but" or "so" when joining two complete sentences.
check: Use a comma before "but" when it joins...
lessons.try: Write sentences using their, there and they're correctly.

learn: Relative pronouns connect extra information: who, whose, whom, which, that.
"The girl who won the race is my sister."
Who for people, which for things.
lessons.try: Combine sentences with relative pronouns.

learn: Relative adverbs: where, when, why.
"The park where we played is closed."
They add details about place, time and reason.
lessons.try: Write five sentences with relative adverbs.

learn: Progressive tenses show ongoing action.
Past: I was running. Present: I am running. Future: I will be running.
Use am, is, are, was, were or will be + -ing.
lessons.try: Write sentences in all three progressive tenses.

learn: Modal verbs show possibility or necessity: can, may, must, should, might.
"You must wear a helmet." "It might rain."
They change the strength of a statement.
lessons.try: Rewrite rules with different modals.

learn: A preposition shows position or time: in, on, under, after, during.
A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition: "under the bridge."
They add detail.
lessons.try: Add prepositional phrases to five sentences.

learn: Complete sentences have a subject and predicate and express a full thought.
Fix fragments by adding missing parts.
Fix run-ons with punctuation or conjunctions.
check: A complete sentence expresses a full...
lessons.try: Fix five fragments and five run-ons.

learn: to/too/two, there/their/they're, its/it's.
Too = also or very. Their = belonging to them. It's = it is.
Read carefully to choose the right one.
lessons.try: Correct ten confused-word errors.

learn: Capitalise proper nouns, first words and titles.
In titles, capitalise important words: The Lion and the Mouse.
Don't capitalise seasons unless at the start.
lessons.try: Fix capitals in a paragraph.

learn: Use a comma before FANBOYS joining two sentences.
"I wanted to go, but it rained."
No comma if only one subject: "I ran and jumped."
check: "I wanted to go, but it rained." The comma comes before...
"I ran and jumped" needs a comma?
lessons.try: Add commas to ten compound sentences.

learn: Use commas to separate speaker tags from quotes.
"Let's go," said Maria. Maria said, "Let's go."
Punctuation goes inside the quotes.
check: Maria said, "Let's go." The comma comes after...
lessons.try: Punctuate a dialogue between three characters.

learn: Use spelling patterns, roots and rules.
Say words slowly and break into syllables.
Check a dictionary when unsure.
lessons.try: Make a personal spelling list of tricky words.

learn: Pronouns, verbs, modals, prepositions and conventions.
Clear grammar makes clear writing.
Edit carefully every time.
lessons.try: Edit a paragraph with ten errors.

units.t: The Writing Process and Types of Writing

learn: The writing process has five steps: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and publishing.
Prewriting includes brainstorming and planning. Drafting is getting ideas down.
Revising improves ideas and organisation; editing fixes conventions.
lessons.try: Take a piece through all five steps.

learn: Opinion writing states a point of view, supports it with reasons and evidence, and ends with a conclusion.
Informative writing explains a topic with facts, definitions and details, grouped logically.
Both use transitions like "for instance", "in addition" and "consequently".
lessons.try: Write an informative paragraph about an animal with a heading and three facts.

learn: A narrative develops real or imagined experiences with descriptive details and clear event order.
Use dialogue and description to show characters' responses.
Use sensory details and a satisfying conclusion.
lessons.try: Write a one-page narrative about a time you felt proud.

learn: Prewriting is planning before drafting.
Brainstorm, list, web or freewrite ideas.
Choose your topic, audience and purpose.
lessons.try: Brainstorm topics and choose one.

learn: Drafting is getting ideas on paper.
Don't worry about perfection.
Follow your plan and keep going.
lessons.try: Draft for 20 minutes without stopping.

learn: Revising improves ideas and organisation.
Add, remove, move or replace (ARMS).
Read aloud to hear problems.
check: ARMS stands for Add, Remove, Move and...
lessons.try: Revise a draft using ARMS.

learn: Editing fixes conventions: capitals, punctuation, spelling.
Use CUPS: Capitals, Usage, Punctuation, Spelling.
Edit last, after revising.
lessons.try: Edit a draft using CUPS.

learn: Publishing shares your final copy.
Make it neat, add a title and visuals.
Share with an audience.
lessons.try: Publish a piece on the class blog or wall.

learn: State a clear opinion.
Give reasons with facts and details.
Use linking words and a conclusion.
lessons.try: Write a four-paragraph opinion essay.

learn: Informative essays explain a topic.
Introduce the topic, group related information, use facts and definitions.
Use headings, formatting and visuals.
lessons.try: Write an informative piece on an animal.

learn: Use precise words and domain-specific vocabulary.
Not "big animal" but "elephant."
Science words make writing exact.
lessons.try: Replace vague words in a draft.

learn: Narratives tell real or imagined experiences.
Use dialogue, description and pacing.
Use transitions to show time.
lessons.try: Write a narrative about a challenge.

learn: Show settings and feelings with senses.
"The salty wind stung my cheeks."
Sensory details pull readers in.
check: "The salty wind stung my cheeks" uses taste and...
lessons.try: Add five sensory details to a narrative.

learn: Read the prompt and underline key words.
Decide the type: opinion, informative or narrative.
Plan quickly, then write.
lessons.try: Respond to a timed prompt.

learn: A portfolio holds your best writing.
Reflect on how you grew this year.
Set goals for next year.
lessons.try: Choose three pieces and write a reflection.
